name: Magda "Screwhead" Szabo

inspiration.oldScript: Hellraiser dressed its demons in leather, chains and piercings, painting kink and leather subculture as literal hell and desire itself as damnation.
inspiration.newLens: Screwhead's horror is control imposed without asking, born of a daughter's grief for her father's store and a lifetime of having to be perfect to be allowed behind the counter. A chain someone chooses is never the villain here, and the Best ending turns on consent, boundaries and a little chaos she finally chooses for herself.

logline: She found the perfect fix for a world that keeps changing: tighten everything until nothing can move, and never ask anyone first. One quarter-turn at a time, Crystal Street is falling into perfect order.
backstory: Laszlo Szabo fled Budapest in 1956 with a toolbox, eleven words of English and a six-year-old daughter named Magda, and by 1960 he had opened a hardware store on Main Street. He painted the sign SZABO & SON because that was what a hardware store was supposed to be called, even though his only child had already sorted every screw in the place. In 1964, the day Magda cut her first perfect key, he climbed a ladder and painted DAUGHTER over SON, and left a little of the old word showing because he liked it when people asked. He sold nails one at a time, fixed anybody's toaster for a quarter and kept a green credit ledger for every family the bank turned away. Magda kept the books from age twelve. She also learned that a woman behind a hardware counter gets asked "Is your father here?" twenty times a day, and that the only answer is to be exactly right, every time, forever. In 1984 Starlight Mall opened with a HomeMax the size of an airplane hangar, and by spring Main Street was boarded up. Laszlo died that summer in the dark, empty store, sorting screws into baby-food jars. Magda took a job at the HomeMax, where a manager half her age put her in Housewares "with the other gals" and rearranged the aisles every month. In October 1985 she bought a brass puzzle box from Oddment and Daughters because the shopkeeper said it "puts things right." She solved it in one night. Now she is Screwhead: gray-streaked hair scraped into a bun pinned with brass screws, a crown of screw heads glinting along her hairline, a tool belt hung with silver chains, and a growing Order of neighbors who smile, stand straight and never change their minds again. She never asks them. She is offering the whole street perfect order. Nothing will ever be lost, because nothing will ever move.

centralIssue.title: Control as grief
centralIssue.summary: Magda is not a monster. She is a daughter who spent her life proving she belonged behind her father's counter, then watched that whole world get bulldozed and decided nothing would ever change again. Tightening the street is how she holds on, and she has stopped asking anyone whether they want to be held. Help her grieve Laszlo, ask before you loosen anything, and remind her that a good fixer knows the difference between a bolt that needs tightening and a person who gets to say stop.

poster: A tall, gaunt woman in her late thirties in a brown shop coat with an orange hardware-store apron over it, gray-streaked dark hair scraped into a tight bun pinned with gleaming brass screws, a crown of brass screw heads along her hairline, silver chains spilling from her tool belt across a suburban street whose houses are snapping into a rigid grid, a glowing brass puzzle box floating in her palm
portrait: Close portrait of a sharp-eyed, grieving woman in her late thirties, gray-streaked dark hair in a severe bun studded with polished brass screws, a neat row of screw heads along her hairline, wire-rimmed reading glasses on a beaded chain, a name tag reading Magda, her face lit gold from below by an open puzzle box, chains glinting in the dark behind her
endingPhoto: A gaunt woman in a brown shop coat and orange hardware-store apron with brass screws pinned through her tight gray-streaked bun, calmly tightening a giant brass screw into a glowing puzzle box on a workbench, hanging chains and pegboard tools swinging around her in a midnight hardware aisle, teens frozen mid-step at the end of the aisle with flashlights
taunts: Lefty loosey, righty tighty. I only go one way now.
Is my father here? No. You'll have to deal with me.
Everything in its place. Everyone in their place. Forever.
My father sold this town one nail at a time. I'll fix it one screw at a time.
I don't ask. Asking is how things come loose.

clues.title: The Szabo & Daughter sign
clues.hint: Joey Benally says somebody comes to Rusty's every night to sort the scrap from a dead hardware store.

encounter.title: The Sorted Pile
encounter.text: Between a crushed Pinto and a tower of bald tires, someone has built something impossible. Every bolt, hinge, drawer pull and doorknob from a gutted store has been sorted by size into a hundred baby-food jars, lined up in rows so straight they hum. Propped against a dead refrigerator above them is a hand-painted sign: SZABO & DAUGHTER HARDWARE. KEYS CUT WHILE YOU WAIT. Under DAUGHTER, if you squint, an older word still shows through: SON.
encounter.art: A junkyard corner at dusk where hundreds of glass jars of sorted screws and hinges stand in perfectly straight rows, a faded hand-painted hardware store sign propped above them with one word painted over an older word, crushed cars looming on either side

choices.label: Ask Joey who has been building it

success.text: Joey rolls out from under a truck and wipes his hands. "Lady named Magda. Shows up at two in the morning, sorts till dawn, barely says a word. First night she told me my wrench grip was wrong. It was." Rusty bought the whole store's fixtures for scrap last year, and last week Joey caught her crying at the crusher, begging Rusty not to flatten the cash register. He shows you where it's hidden, under a tarp: brass, dented, still ringing.
success.art: A teen mechanic lifting a tarp off an old brass cash register hidden in a junkyard, a hardware store sign behind him, a flashlight beam cutting through dusk

failure.text: Joey is elbow-deep in a transmission and tells you to come back when you can tell a socket from a spanner. As you walk away, every lid on every jar turns a quarter-turn at once with a single, perfect click.
failure.art: Rows of glass jars in a dark junkyard, every lid twisting at once, a teenager freezing mid-step in the foreground

choices.label: Read the labels on every jar

success.text: Each jar is labeled twice: once in an old man's spidery Hungarian, and once below it in a woman's precise block capitals that copy the first exactly, down to his spelling mistakes. The last jar is labeled only in the old hand: APA'S LAST SORT, JUNE 1985. It is half full. Someone has never been able to bring herself to finish it.
success.art: A flashlight beam on a single half-full baby-food jar of screws, its label written in shaky old-fashioned handwriting, a row of identical jars stretching into the dark

failure.text: Your elbow knocks a jar off the row. The screws scatter across the dirt, then roll uphill, back into the jar, one by one, and the lid screws itself on. Somewhere deep in the car maze a chain begins to drag.
failure.art: Screws rolling uphill across junkyard dirt back into a toppled glass jar, a frightened teenager backing away, a chain trailing into a maze of stacked cars

choices.label: Take one screw out of its jar on purpose

success.text: You pocket a single wood screw. The whole shrine shudders, and for one second the junkyard fills with an old man's laugh and a voice with a thick accent: "Lefty loosey, Magdi! Not everything has to be tight! Not even you!" The sign is warm when you touch it, like it remembers a hand on a ladder, a brush, a fresh coat of paint.
success.art: A teenager holding up a single screw in a junkyard while a ghostly old shopkeeper in a brown coat laughs behind the rows of jars, faint and golden

failure.text: Your fingers lock around the jar. You cannot open your hand. You stand there until the sun goes down and a silver chain loops softly around your ankle, and only Barnaby's howl from the front gate breaks you free.
failure.art: A teenager frozen with a hand clamped around a glass jar at sunset, a thin silver chain curling around their ankle from the shadows

clues.title: The Szabos' credit book
clues.hint: Pearl Washington has lived on Crystal Street since 1959 and remembers every shopkeeper who treated her fairly.

encounter.title: The Credit Book
encounter.text: Pearl's rocking chair creaks while she cleans a rock-salt shotgun across her knees. When you say the name Szabo, she stops rocking. "Laszlo," she says. "Now there was a man who never once made me wait while he served somebody whiter first. And his girl Magda was the same, only faster." She has a cigar box inside she has never shown anyone.
encounter.art: An elderly Black woman in a cardigan on a porch rocker with a shotgun across her knees, an old cigar box on the side table, autumn leaves on the lawn of a split-level house

choices.label: Settle on the porch step and let her tell it her way

success.text: 1962: new widow, two kids, a bank manager who laughed at her. Laszlo opened a green ledger and wrote her name. "Pay when you can." The book has four hundred names in it, and from 1962 on, every entry is in Magda's tidy hand. On the night the store closed Laszlo crossed out every single debt in his own: FORGIVEN. "She kept that book better than any bank for twenty years," Pearl says. "Then she stood there and watched her daddy forgive the whole town in one night. And then the girl went and sat in the dark."
success.art: An open green credit ledger on a porch table, neat rows of names crossed out with the word forgiven in old ink, an elderly woman's finger resting on one name

failure.text: Pearl drifts into a different story, about a radio set in 1944 that picked up voices from a ship that had already sunk. It is a fantastic story. It is not this one. By the time it ends it's dusk, and across the street the Delgados are standing perfectly straight on their lawn, not blinking.
failure.art: Dusk on a cul-de-sac, a married couple standing rigid and unblinking on their front lawn, a teenager and an old woman on a porch across the street watching uneasily

choices.label: Offer to fix her sagging screen door while she talks

success.text: Pearl hands you a screwdriver from her kitchen drawer, its wooden handle worn smooth and stamped SZABO & DAUGHTER. While you work she brings out the cigar box: the green ledger, and a snapshot of Laszlo and a teenage Magda behind the counter, both laughing, the girl holding up the first key she ever cut, the new sign above them with the paint still wet.
success.art: A faded snapshot of a laughing old shopkeeper and a grinning teenage girl in braids behind a hardware counter, the girl holding up a freshly cut key, a freshly painted shop sign above them, a worn screwdriver beside the photo

failure.text: The screw strips and the whole door sags off its hinge. Pearl laughs until she wheezes. "Laszlo would've had that done in thirty seconds. Magda in twenty." Overnight, every screw in her door tightens itself so hard that by morning it won't open at all.
failure.art: A screen door hanging crooked from one hinge on a porch, an old woman laughing in her rocker, a teenager holding a stripped screw in dismay

clues.title: The letter under the level
clues.hint: Laszlo Szabo is buried at Pinecrest, and Father Iggy says his grave is the neatest thing he's ever seen, and not in a good way.

encounter.title: Plot 112, Perfectly Level
encounter.text: Every grave in Pinecrest leans a little, like old teeth. Except one. Laszlo Szabo's headstone is plumb to the degree, the grass around it trimmed with scissors, the gravel sorted by color. A brass level sits on top of the stone, its bubble dead center. Fresh chrysanthemums stand in a perfect grid. Nearby, Father Iggy pretends to tune his bass.
encounter.art: An autumn cemetery of crooked old headstones, one grave perfectly straight and manicured with sorted gravel and gridded flowers, a brass level on top of the stone, a priest with a bass guitar watching from a bench

choices.label: Ask Father Iggy about the woman who visits

success.text: "Magda," Iggy says. "Every dawn. Never prays. Just measures. At the funeral the undertaker asked if there was a son to help with the casket, and she lowered it herself, and wouldn't let it go until the straps were even. Took forty minutes." He digs out the program. Laszlo asked for his own words to be printed on the back: Things break. We fix what we can. The rest, we let go, and then we eat dinner.
success.art: A young priest in a clerical collar and a punk band T-shirt handing a folded funeral program to a teenager beside a perfectly level headstone

failure.text: Iggy is in the middle of a very serious funeral for somebody's hamster and shushes you. You wander off between the stones and find a fresh one, perfectly level, perfectly blank, with a brass level resting on top. It is exactly your height.
failure.art: A blank, freshly cut headstone standing perfectly straight among crooked old graves, a brass level on top, a teenager staring at it

choices.label: Lift the brass level off the headstone

success.text: Under the level is an envelope addressed MAGDI in an old man's hand, rain-stained, never opened. You read it, and you're sorry, Magda. "I am not sad, kislányom. A store is only a box. The town was the thing, and the town is still here. You never had to be perfect for me. You only had to be there, and you always were. Don't you dare spend your life keeping my shelves."
success.art: A weathered envelope addressed in shaky handwriting lying open on a headstone, a brass level set aside, a teenager reading a letter in morning mist

failure.text: The moment the level leaves the stone, every headstone in Pinecrest straightens at once with a grinding groan, a whole cemetery snapping to attention. The air smells like machine oil, and you run.
failure.art: An entire cemetery of headstones grinding upright at the same instant, dust and leaves flying, a teenager sprinting between the rows

signature.title: Aisle Nine Goes On Forever
signature.place: A HomeMax that isn't there, 2 a.m.
signature.text: You walked out for a Bolt Cola and walked into a hardware store that should be the 7-Eleven. Orange aisles stretch to a vanishing point under humming fluorescent light. Every item is faced, priced and identical. A calm voice like a dentist's comes over the PA: "Attention shoppers. Please remain in your aisle. Order is being restored." Far down Aisle Nine, a tall woman with a crown of brass screws is restocking, and she does not look up.
signature.art: An endless big-box hardware store aisle under harsh fluorescent light, identical products faced in perfect rows, a lone teenager in pajamas and sneakers, a distant tall woman with brass screws pinned through her hair stocking shelves

choices.label: Sprint for the exit sign before the aisles slide

success.text: You cut through Housewares, slide under a pallet as two aisles grind together like a sliding puzzle, and burst out of the automatic doors into the cold parking lot of the 7-Eleven. In your fist is a single brass screw, warm as a pulse.
success.art: A teenager diving through closing automatic doors into a night parking lot as the shelves behind them slide shut like puzzle tiles, a brass screw glinting in their hand

failure.text: The aisles close like a sliding puzzle. You turn a corner into Aisle Nine. Again. And again. You get out at dawn, but your pockets have been perfectly organized, coins by year, and you can't remember doing it.
failure.art: A dizzy teenager at the end of an identical hardware aisle with an aisle nine sign overhead, coins stacked neatly by year in their open palm

choices.label: Knock every can of paint off the shelves

success.text: Thirty colors explode across the spotless floor: tangerine, teal, a purple called Midnight Rendezvous. The PA screams static. Disorder tears through the store like wet paper and you wake up in the 7-Eleven lot, splattered teal, cackling.
success.art: Paint cans bursting across a perfect hardware store floor in splashes of tangerine, teal and purple, the shelves tearing apart like wet paper, a delighted teenager in the middle

failure.text: Every can you shove lands upright, label forward. A soft chain loops your ankle. "Thank you for shopping," says the PA. You come to in a parked car with your seatbelt fastened, very, very tight.
failure.art: Paint cans landing perfectly upright on a gleaming floor, labels facing forward, a silver chain curling around a sneaker

choices.label: Ask the clerk, politely, where they keep the tools for loosening

success.text: She stops. The screws in her crown catch the light. Nobody in this store has asked her a real question in a year. "We don't... stock those anymore," she says, and for one second she looks like a tired woman in an orange apron who hasn't slept since summer. She points you to the exit without a word.
success.art: A gaunt woman clerk in an orange apron with brass screws pinned through her bun pausing mid-restock, her face suddenly sad and human, pointing a teenager toward a glowing exit

failure.text: "Everything you need is in your aisle," she says, without turning around. Your jacket zipper zips itself to your chin, and your shoelaces knot themselves into perfect, impossible double bows.
failure.art: A teenager's jacket zipper sliding up by itself under fluorescent light, shoelaces tying themselves into bows, a woman clerk's back turned in the distance

signature.title: The Leveling
signature.text: You wake to a sound like a thousand ratchets. Out your window, Crystal Street is rearranging itself: the houses grinding on their foundations into a perfect grid, crooked mailboxes snapping plumb, the round Heartstone garden squaring off into a box. Neighbors stand at their mailboxes in pajamas with silver chains looped kindly around their wrists. Even Mr. and Mr. Abernathy-Cole, who mow in zigzags on principle, are standing at attention. "Nobody asked us," one of them says through a fixed smile, "but it's fine." "It doesn't hurt," calls Mrs. Delgado. "Nothing moves. Isn't it wonderful?"
signature.art: A suburban cul-de-sac at midnight with houses grinding into a rigid grid, mailboxes snapping straight, neighbors in pajamas standing chained at their mailboxes with peaceful smiles, a purple geode in a garden that is turning square

choices.label: Go house to house and ask each neighbor if they want out

success.text: You ask each of them out loud: "Do you want this off?" It takes a while for anyone to find the word, but every neighbor who manages a yes, their chain goes slack with a little sigh. Mrs. Delgado blinks and asks why she's on the lawn in her curlers. The Abernathy-Coles immediately go back to bickering about the hedges, and three houses grind back to their crooked, perfect places.
success.art: A teenager twisting a silver chain loose from a woman's wrist at a mailbox, the chain falling slack, two men in bathrobes arguing happily behind them as houses settle back askew

failure.text: You loosen one link and it tightens on you instead. You spend the rest of the night chained gently to the Delgados' mailbox, watching the street square itself. The morning paper calls it a freak frost heave.
failure.art: A teenager chained by one wrist to a suburban mailbox at dawn, the street behind them laid out in an eerie perfect grid, a newspaper on the lawn

choices.label: Crank a boombox and get everyone dancing badly

success.text: You put on the loudest thing you own and do the worst Running Man in Glimmer Falls history. Nobody can stay level while they're laughing. The Abernathy-Coles start voguing. Mrs. Delgado does the Bump. Chains clatter off wrists onto the asphalt. Order cannot survive the Electric Slide.
success.art: Neighbors in pajamas dancing wildly on a cul-de-sac at midnight around a blaring boombox, silver chains dropping off their wrists, a teenager in glow bracelets leading the chaos

failure.text: They dance. All of them, in perfect unison, precise as a drill team, smiling the same smile. You are the only one off the beat, and on the next count every head on Crystal Street turns to look at you.
failure.art: Rows of neighbors in pajamas dancing in flawless unison on a gridded street, every head turned toward one teenager holding a boombox

signature.title: The Box Solves Itself
signature.text: The brass puzzle box is on your nightstand. You never brought it home. It's turning by itself, panels clicking and sliding, each click a little louder, and with every click your room gets neater: posters squared, sheets tucked hospital-tight, cassettes alphabetized. From a seam of gold light, chains begin to unspool across the walls, and a woman's voice like a store intercom says, "One more turn and you'll never lose anything again. You don't have to say yes. I've already decided."
signature.art: A cluttered 1980s teenage bedroom snapping into eerie neatness, a brass puzzle box glowing gold on the nightstand, silver chains unspooling from a seam of light across shelves and walls

choices.label: Grab the box and hold its panels still

success.text: The panels grind against your palms like a living thing. You hold on. The last panel strains, shudders, and stops a hair from closing. The chains retract with a sulky rattle, and your room explodes back into its glorious mess.
success.art: A teenager gripping a glowing brass puzzle box with both hands, knuckles white, chains snapping back into the walls, laundry and cassettes tumbling back into disorder

failure.text: The box completes its turn. You wake to a perfect room and one thin silver chain looped around your wrist, too tight to slip off and too loose to hurt. You find yourself making your bed without deciding to.
failure.art: A teenager sitting on a perfectly made bed in an eerily tidy room, staring at a thin silver chain around their wrist, a closed brass box on the nightstand

choices.label: Solve the box backward, lefty loosey

success.text: You turn every panel the wrong way. The box unravels with a sound like a long-held breath let out. Inside there are no chains, only a small brass key tag stamped SZABO & DAUGHTER. KEYS CUT WHILE YOU WAIT. It feels like something somebody was meant to find.
success.art: An unfolded brass puzzle box lying open and harmless on a bedspread, a small brass key tag inside catching the lamplight, a teenager leaning over it in wonder

failure.text: The panels reverse under your fingers and solve themselves twice as fast. Your shoelaces tie into knots it will take a week to undo, and every drawer in your room locks with a satisfied click.
failure.art: A brass puzzle box spinning its panels in a blur under a teenager's frantic fingers, dresser drawers slamming shut around the room

choices.label: Open the window and hurl it as far as you can

success.text: It sails over the fence, over the Delgados' roof, and lands somewhere far off with a clang like a dropped toolbox. The chains snap back into the wall. It'll be back. But not tonight.
success.art: A teenager leaning out a bedroom window having just hurled a glowing brass box into the night sky over suburban rooftops, chains whipping back into the room

failure.text: You throw it hard. You hear it land. Then you hear it coming back, click by click, up the drainpipe, across the roof. When you turn around it is on your nightstand again, polished, warm and one turn closer.
failure.art: A brass puzzle box sitting back on a nightstand, gleaming, while a frightened teenager stands at an open window staring at it

finale.title: Closing Time at Szabo & Daughter
finale.text: On Halloween the Heartstone opens like a puzzle box and Crystal Street folds inside it. You stand in a perfect copy of Szabo & Daughter Hardware, every drawer labeled in her precise capitals, every neighbor standing in an aisle with a silver chain around their wrist, smiling. Behind the counter Magda works a key-cutting wheel that throws sparks like fireworks. She wears her HomeMax apron over her father's brown shop coat, the sleeves rolled twice. "Nothing will ever close again," she says. "Not on my watch. And nobody will ever walk in here again and ask me if my father is around."
finale.art: A vast impossible hardware store inside a glowing purple geode, endless labeled drawers, chained smiling neighbors in every aisle, a tall woman with brass screws pinned through her bun behind a counter cutting keys in a shower of sparks, a teen crew in Halloween costumes facing her

choices.label: Throw the breaker and wreck the key machine

success.text: Sparks, a bang, darkness. The perfect store rattles apart into ten thousand loose screws that rain down onto the roundabout grass. Screwhead falls with them, and lands as just a woman in an orange apron, asleep on the lawn, remembering nothing at all.
success.art: A key-cutting machine exploding in sparks as a hardware store bursts apart into a rain of screws over a suburban roundabout, a woman in an apron collapsing asleep on the grass

failure.text: The machine won't stop. Chains loop around your wrists, soft and certain as a seatbelt. "There," she says gently, almost kindly, and she does not ask. "Now you're safe."
failure.art: Silver chains wrapping a struggling teenager's wrists in front of a sparking key machine, a tall woman with a crown of brass screws looking down at them with pity

choices.label: Swap the labels on one drawer and let her try to fix it

success.text: You swap the quarter-inch and the three-eighths. She can't stand it. She fixes it. You swap two more. The crew starts swapping every label in the store, and she spins in place trying to correct everything at once until the box can't hold its own disorder and pops open, spilling the whole street out onto the lawn.
success.art: A teen crew frantically swapping labels on hundreds of hardware drawers while a woman with brass screws in her hair spins in panic trying to fix them, the walls of the store cracking open to the night sky

failure.text: She sees you do it. "I was doing my father's inventory at twelve, kid." Every drawer in the store slams shut at once like a giant clapping its hands, and your fingers are caught in one of them.
failure.art: Hundreds of drawers slamming shut at once along an endless wall, a teenager's hand caught in one, a woman behind the counter shaking her head

choices.label: Show her the sign, the ledger and her father's letter, then ask before you loosen anything

success.text: You set the old sign on the counter, open the green ledger to FORGIVEN, and read Laszlo's letter out loud. Magda's hands stop on the wheel. "He forgave all of them," she says. "Even the ones who went to the mall." You hold out your hand, palm up, and ask: "Can I loosen one?" Nobody has asked her anything in a year. She stares at you, then nods. One screw comes out of her crown, then another, falling ringing to the floor. "A chain somebody chooses is a promise," she says slowly. "One you put on them is a cage." She takes off the orange apron and goes aisle to aisle, asking each neighbor, "Do you want this off?", and turning each chain a quarter-turn the other way when they say yes.
success.art: A tearful woman reading an old letter at a hardware counter as brass screws fall from her loosened hair like rain, an open green ledger and a hand-painted sign before her, a teenager holding out an open palm, freed neighbors rubbing their wrists

failure.text: She grips the counter until it creaks. "Words don't hold anything together." You have everything she needs to hear, but she's wound too tight to hear it yet, and the whole store groans like a ship.
failure.art: A woman with a crown of brass screws gripping a hardware counter with white knuckles, a teenager holding out a letter, the store walls straining and bending

best.title: Keys Cut While You Wait
best.text: On November first Magda goes to Pinecrest and loosens her father's headstone a single quarter-turn so it can lean like everybody else's. Then she goes home and eats dinner. By December there's a card table at the Heartstone roundabout every Saturday: SZABO & DAUGHTER FIX-IT, painted crooked on purpose. Toasters, Walkmans, bike chains, a quarter each, pay when you can, and she asks before she fixes anything, because some people like their things a little broken. She keeps a green ledger. She lets the crew rearrange her toolbox however they want and only twitches a little. On Friday nights she leaves the table to Frankie, borrows Wade's leather jacket and goes dancing at the Glitter Box with her hair down and every screw out. She teaches you to cut a key, and the first one you make opens nothing at all, and she says that's fine, she'll keep it anyway.
best.art: A smiling woman in a brown shop coat with loose gray-streaked hair at a card table repair stand by a purple geode on a suburban roundabout, a crookedly painted sign above her, teens and neighbors lined up with broken toasters and boomboxes, a green ledger open beside her

good.title: Everything in Its Place
good.text: The store dissolves, the chains fall away, and Crystal Street wakes up with its houses back where they belong, slightly crooked. Magda goes back to the HomeMax and her orange apron. Sometimes, driving past at three a.m., you see her alone in a lit aisle straightening a display that was already straight, and you wonder what it was she lost, and who she had to be to keep it.
good.art: A lone woman in an orange apron straightening a perfect display in a brightly lit, empty big-box store at night, seen through the glass doors from a dark parking lot

bittersweet.title: A Quarter-Turn Too Tight
bittersweet.text: You survive the week and so does most of the street, but a few neighbors never quite loosen up. The Delgados mow their lawn in perfect stripes at six a.m. every day now and never laugh at the same jokes twice. Magda moves away in the spring without saying goodbye. On your wrist there's a faint white line where a chain once was, and on bad days it itches like a screw being turned.
bittersweet.art: A suburban lawn mowed in eerily perfect stripes at dawn, a stiff couple standing on the porch, a teenager on the sidewalk rubbing a faint pale line on their wrist

bad.title: Perfect Order
bad.text: You wake on November first and your life is perfectly organized. Your tapes are alphabetized. Your hair is combed. Every evening at six you stand at your mailbox with your hands folded and wait for nothing in particular. Nobody asked you, and you can't remember how to say stop. Your crew tries to make you laugh. You check your watch, and you smile, and you don't move at all.
bad.art: A teenager with neatly combed hair standing perfectly still at a mailbox at dusk with folded hands and a calm smile, friends in colorful costumes trying desperately to get their attention
